title: The index is not sequential
description: The *index* comes from the middle bits of an address, so addresses far apart can land in the *same set*.

steps.text: The set is chosen by the 3 *index* bits, bits 4 to 6 of the address. Counting up through addresses walks through the sets and then wraps round, as the next few loads show.

steps.hint: Type `0x000` in the address box (do not issue it) and read bits 4 to 6 in the strip.

steps.explain: Set 1. `0x010` is 16 bytes on, one whole line, so the index went up by one.
steps.hint: Each line is 16 bytes, which is `0x10`.

steps.explain: Set 0 again. `0x100` is `1 0000 0000`: the index bits (4 to 6) are `000`, and the extra `1` is part of the *tag*.
steps.hint: Do not count up. Read bits 4 to 6 of `0x100`. Most of its bits are zero.

steps.text: `0x100` went into set 0, where `0x000` was. This cache has one way per set, so the new line took its place.

steps.explain: Set 1, shared with `0x010`. Same index bits, different tag.
steps.hint: `0x110` differs from `0x010` only in the tag bits.

steps.text: Now try one yourself. Load from `0x080`. Which set will it use?
steps.hint: Type `0x080` in the address box and press Issue.

steps.text: Set 0 again. The cache is 128 bytes (`0x80`) in size, so addresses that are a multiple of that apart always share a set. Next module: what happens when they take turns.
